clickjacking-and-csp-frame-ancestors.htm.text:
Why X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM doesn't protect you anymore

Clickjacking works by loading your page inside an invisible or disguised <iframe> on an attacker's site, then tricking a visitor into clicking something that is really a button on your page underneath -- a "log in with Google" prompt, a "confirm transfer" button, a cookie-consent toggle. The defence is telling the browser which sites, if any, are allowed to frame your page at all, and two different headers can say so.

frame-ancestors does not fall back to default-src

Most Content-Security-Policy directives that control where a resource can load from -- script-src, img-src, connect-src, and others -- fall back to default-src when they aren't explicitly set. frame-ancestors is a navigation directive, not a fetch directive, and the CSP specification does not give it that fallback. A policy of default-src 'self' alone gives the page no clickjacking protection from CSP -- the directive has to be spelled out on its own.

Three states, and only one header combination tells you which

What's presentActually protected in current browsers?
CSP frame-ancestors set (to anything but *)Yes -- takes precedence over X-Frame-Options everywhere
No frame-ancestors, but X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGINYes
No frame-ancestors, only X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM https://example.comNo -- every current major browser engine ignores the ALLOW-FROM value entirely
Neither header presentNo

The third row is the one worth checking for by name: it is the only case where a header is present, looks correct, and still leaves the page completely unprotected -- a raw curl -I dump reads it as "has X-Frame-Options" with no way to tell that a browser will not honour it.

Check your own site automatically

The checker on this site sends one real request, applies these CSP fallback and ALLOW-FROM rules, and reports which of the three states above your response is in -- plus whether your CSP's effective script-src allows 'unsafe-inline' with no nonce or hash to override it, or a wildcard host source, and whether the response has Strict-Transport-Security at all. The request comes from a Node CLI you run yourself against a system you own or are authorised to test; the browser page only renders a report you paste in.

This is evidence from that one response, not a full security assessment -- see the checker and its disclaimer for what it does and doesn't cover.

← Back to the checker

It is not security advice, and it does not replace a qualified security review or penetration test. index.html.text:
Security Headers Checker

Sends one real HTTP GET request to a URL you choose and classifies the response's frame-protection and Content-Security-Policy headers into well-documented misconfiguration patterns: missing clickjacking protection, X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM (a value every current browser silently ignores), a CSP script-src allowing 'unsafe-inline' with no nonce or hash to override it, a CSP wildcard script source, CSP shipped only as report-only, and a missing Strict-Transport-Security header. Only point it at a system you own or are authorised to test.

1. Run the CLI against your site

Node.js, no dependencies to install:

node check.mjs https://example.com --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the URL you pass; nothing goes through this site.

2. Paste the JSON output here

Paste the JSON from step 1 and click Check.

Report

Raw response headers

Common questions

What does a missing frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options header let an attacker do?

Without either header, any site on the web can load your page inside an iframe and overlay it, tricking a visitor into clicking a button on your page while believing they're clicking something else -- clickjacking. It can turn a 'log in with Google' click, a funds-transfer confirmation, or a cookie-consent toggle into an action the visitor never meant to take.

Why does X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM show up as a danger finding instead of protected?

Every current major browser engine dropped support for the ALLOW-FROM value once CSP2's frame-ancestors directive shipped as the replacement. A response sending it looks protected in a raw header dump, but no browser in real use today actually honours it -- the page has no frame protection at all unless a CSP frame-ancestors directive is also present.

Does CSP frame-ancestors inherit from default-src the way script-src does?

No. Most CSP fetch directives fall back to default-src when they're not explicitly set, but frame-ancestors is a navigation directive and the spec does not give it that fallback. A policy of default-src 'self' alone provides zero clickjacking protection -- frame-ancestors has to be spelled out on its own. More background: why X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM doesn't protect you anymore.

Why does 'unsafe-inline' only count as a finding when there's no nonce or hash?

CSP2 and later browsers ignore 'unsafe-inline' entirely whenever a nonce-source or hash-source is also present in the same directive -- it's kept in the header only so CSP1-era browsers still get some protection. So a script-src carrying both a nonce and 'unsafe-inline' is correctly configured for every browser that matters today; this tool only flags 'unsafe-inline' when nothing overrides it.

Why does this need a CLI instead of just checking a URL I type into the page?

Nothing stops a browser page from making the request itself for a same-origin target, but checking an arbitrary third-party URL from inside a browser tab runs into the same CORS and mixed-content restrictions the page you're checking is designed to resist -- and a page that could reach any URL you type would itself be a server-side request forgery risk. A small local CLI with no such restriction, run from your own machine, is the same shape every other tool in this class (curl, securityheaders-style scanners) uses.

Does a clean report mean the site has no security-header issues?

No. This checks a specific, well-documented set of frame-protection, CSP-strength, and HSTS patterns from one response -- it is not a full security assessment, does not crawl other pages on the site, and cannot see a misconfiguration this tool's checks don't happen to cover (Permissions-Policy and Referrer-Policy, cookie flags, and Subresource Integrity, for instance, are out of scope here -- see referrer-permissions-policy-check for the first two and sri-check for the last). Treat a clean report as evidence about these specific patterns, not a determination that the site is secure.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks a specific, well-documented set of frame-protection, CSP-strength, and HSTS patterns from one response. It is not a full security assessment, does not crawl other pages on the site, and cannot see a pattern it doesn't check for. A clean report describes what this one request found, not a guarantee the site has no security-header issues.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not security advice, and it does not replace a qualified security review or penetration test. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for having authorisation to test any system you point the CLI at. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Do not use it as a system of record.

Nothing leaves your browser. The CLI's request goes straight from your machine to the URL you name -- never through this site. The page you're reading now only parses JSON you paste into it locally; nothing is uploaded. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day -- no target URLs, no response headers, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor. Turn it off with the checkbox above.

Free and open source. The code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

Also worth a pass on your API: CORS misconfiguration checker covers a different response-header evidence class (a reflected Origin rather than a frame or script policy), Subresource Integrity checker covers a script tag's own hash against what a CDN actually serves, and Cookie Security checker covers Set-Cookie attributes -- SameSite=None without Secure and broken __Host-/__Secure- prefixes -- which this tool deliberately leaves out of scope, and Cache-Control checker covers HTTP caching headers (Vary, Cache-Control, ETag) -- a fifth response-header evidence class, also out of scope here.

And once the headers are right, the other thing a stranger looks for on your site is where to report what they found: security.txt checker validates your /.well-known/security.txt against RFC 9116. Worth running on a schedule rather than once -- the RFC makes Expires mandatory, so a valid file becomes an invalid one on its own, while still serving a 200.

Prefer a hosted, single-grade outside read of a public site instead? See how this checker compares to Security Headers (securityheaders.com) -- different shapes, and when to reach for each. Already have DevTools open? See how this checker compares to checking headers by eye in DevTools.

This tool's own CSP and clickjacking checks stop at frame and script policy -- for where a page's outbound Referer goes and which powerful features (camera, microphone, geolocation) a page and its embedded third parties may use, see Referrer-Policy & Permissions-Policy checker, the same one-request, plain-English-report shape as this tool.

vs-checking-headers-by-eye-in-devtools.h.text:
← Security Headers Checker

This checker vs. checking headers by eye in DevTools

Browser DevTools -- the Network tab's Headers panel -- shows the raw response headers for a request you've already made, for free, with nothing to install. It is a fine first look at what a server actually sent, and for a page you're already inspecting it is often the fastest option there is. What it does not do is apply the fallback rules that decide whether those headers actually protect anything: that a CSP frame-ancestors directive does not inherit from default-src the way script-src does, so a policy of default-src 'self' alone gives zero clickjacking protection, or that an X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM value looks like frame protection in the panel and is silently ignored by every current browser engine. Reading raw headers in a panel and knowing which combinations quietly fail are two different skills.

This tool sends one request to a URL you name and classifies the response's frame-protection, CSP-strength, and HSTS headers into named patterns -- missing clickjacking protection, the dead ALLOW-FROM value, a CSP script-src allowing 'unsafe-inline' with nothing overriding it, a wildcard script source, CSP shipped only as report-only, and a missing Strict-Transport-Security header -- stating in plain English which header proves each one. It does not replace DevTools -- for a page open in your browser right now, the Network tab is still the quickest way to glance at a response. It automates the fallback-rule reasoning a person would otherwise have to redo by eye, every time, and it runs from a terminal or CI job where clicking through a Network tab isn't practical.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I have a page open in my browser and want a quick look at its response headers. DevTools' Network tab -- that quick raw look is exactly its job.
I want to know whether frame-protection and CSP headers actually protect against clickjacking, applying the correct fallback rules. This checker -- frame-ancestors does not inherit from default-src; a naive read of the panel can miss that.
I want to know whether an X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM value I can see in the panel is actually doing anything. This checker -- names it as ignored by every current major browser instead of leaving you to look that up.
I want this checked automatically on every deploy, with a non-zero exit code on a real problem. This checker's CLI -- node check.mjs <url> --json exits non-zero on a danger-severity finding. DevTools has no CLI to wire into CI.
I'd rather not re-derive the CSP fallback rules from memory to read a headers panel myself. This checker -- paste the CLI's JSON into the browser report and get the plain-English findings without already knowing the rules.

Neither tool replaces the other, and in practice most people use both: DevTools for a fast raw look at one response you're already looking at, this tool for the recurring, automatable question of whether that response's frame-protection, CSP, and HSTS headers actually do what they look like they do.

Try it

node check.mjs https://example.com --json

One request to the URL you name, the same kind your browser already sends. Paste the JSON into the checker for the plain-English report.

Common questions

Should I use this tool instead of DevTools?

Different jobs, and most people who use this tool also still open DevTools. The Network tab's Headers panel shows you the raw response headers for a request you've already made in your browser -- free, already installed, and often the fastest way to check one page you're looking at anyway. It does not tell you which of those headers, read together, form a well-documented weakness: whether an X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM value is silently ignored by every current browser, or whether a CSP's frame-ancestors is missing because default-src alone does not cover it. This tool reads the same headers DevTools would show you and names the specific, well-documented pattern -- so you don't have to already know the CSP fallback rules to notice the problem.

Why would I need more than DevTools if I already know what to look for?

If you already know that frame-ancestors doesn't inherit from default-src the way script-src does, that ALLOW-FROM is dead in every current browser, and that unsafe-inline is only a real gap when nothing overrides it, DevTools plus your own judgement is enough. This tool exists for the times you don't want to re-derive those rules from memory on every response, or when you want the same checks wired into your own CI as a non-zero exit code, which DevTools' UI cannot do -- it has no CLI and nothing to script against.

Does this tool see anything DevTools can't?

No -- it sees the same response headers DevTools already shows you, and nothing more. The difference is entirely in the reading: this tool applies the frame-protection, CSP-strength, and HSTS checks the same way every time, whether or not you remember the fallback rules, and it can run from a terminal or a CI job where opening a browser and clicking through the Network tab isn't practical.

Is my target URL or its response headers uploaded anywhere?

No. The CLI's request goes directly from your machine to the URL you name, exactly like the request your browser already makes. The browser report viewer only parses JSON you paste into it yourself, locally in your browser -- nothing about the target, the headers, or the report is sent anywhere. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used, with no target URLs or header values in it.

Want a hosted, single-grade outside read instead? See this checker vs. Security Headers (securityheaders.com).

Evidence, not a determination. This checks a specific, well-documented set of frame-protection, CSP-strength, and HSTS patterns from one response. It is not a full security assessment and cannot see a pattern it doesn't check for.

To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

vs-securityheaders.html.text:
← Security Headers Checker

This checker vs. Security Headers (securityheaders.com)

Security Headers, at securityheaders.com and run by security researcher Scott Helme, is one of the best-known free tools in this space. You give it a URL, its own server fetches the live response, and it hands back a single letter grade -- A+ down to F -- summarising the site's overall header hygiene. It needs nothing installed and no account, and for a quick outside read on a public site it is a genuinely useful first stop.

This checker does a narrower, differently-shaped job. It is a single zero-dependency Node CLI: node check.mjs <url> sends one request from your own machine (not from a third party's server) and classifies the response's frame-protection and Content-Security-Policy headers into named misconfiguration patterns -- missing clickjacking protection, an X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM value every current major browser silently ignores, a CSP script-src allowing 'unsafe-inline' with nothing overriding it, a wildcard script source, CSP shipped only as report-only, and a missing Strict-Transport-Security header -- rather than folding everything into one grade. It has no server-side component of its own: the browser page here only renders a report from JSON you already have.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Get a quick, single-grade outside read on a public site's overall header hygiene. Security Headers -- one paste, one grade, no install.
Check a private, password-protected, or staging URL your machine can reach but a public third-party server cannot. This checker -- the CLI makes the request from wherever you run it.
Know exactly why a finding is a finding -- for example that ALLOW-FROM looks like frame protection but no current browser honours it, or that frame-ancestors does not inherit from default-src the way script-src does. This checker -- named patterns and the exact header behind each one, not a single grade.
Make sure the URL and response headers you're checking never pass through any third party at all. This checker -- the request goes straight from your machine to the target; the browser page only parses JSON you paste into it locally.
Gate a deploy in your own CI on a specific clickjacking/CSP/HSTS regression with an exit code. This checker -- node check.mjs <url> exits non-zero on a danger finding.
See how the full, broader set of modern security headers (Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, and others this checker doesn't cover) reads on a public site, in one view. Security Headers -- this checker only covers frame protection, CSP strength, and HSTS.

These compose rather than compete. A reasonable habit is Security Headers for a fast outside sanity check on a site that's already public, and this checker wired into your own CI against your own staging environment, where a regression in the specific patterns it covers turns a build red the day it lands rather than being caught later by a public scan. Neither one replaces the other.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Security Headers (securityheaders.com)?

They can both be useful, and for a quick outside read on a public site, Security Headers is a reasonable first stop. It is a free, well-known web scanner: you give it a URL, its own server fetches the response, and it returns a single letter grade (A+ down to F) based on which security headers are present. This checker does something narrower and more specific: a local Node CLI you run yourself sends one request to a URL you name, from your own machine, and classifies the frame-protection and CSP headers into named patterns -- including the ALLOW-FROM trap and the frame-ancestors/default-src fallback distinction -- rather than a single overall grade. Reach for Security Headers for a fast outside opinion on a public site; reach for this when you want a plain-English reason for a clickjacking or CSP-strength finding, or a check you can run unattended against a private staging URL.

Security Headers is free too -- what does this add?

Being free is not the difference. The differences are who makes the request and what the output actually explains. Security Headers' own server fetches your URL, which is fine for a public production site but means a private, password-protected, or staging URL either can't be scanned or has to be reachable from the public internet for a third party to reach it. This checker's CLI runs on your own machine (or your own CI runner) and sends the request itself -- it can point at localhost, a VPN-only staging host, or anything else your machine can reach, and nothing about the target URL or the response ever goes through this site or any other third party. And where a grade tells you a header is missing, this checker's report names the exact header and the specific rule it fails -- for example that an X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM value is present but silently ignored by every current browser, or that a CSP's unsafe-inline is a real gap because no nonce or hash overrides it.

Why does this need a CLI instead of one paste-a-URL box like Security Headers?

Because a browser page that could fetch any URL you typed into it would itself be a server-side request forgery risk, and it would rule out exactly the private and staging URLs a developer most wants to check before a site goes public. Security Headers solves that by making the request from its own server, which is the right tradeoff for a public site you're happy for a third party to fetch. This checker makes the opposite tradeoff: the request comes from a small local CLI you run yourself, and the browser page here only renders the JSON you already have -- nothing typed into it is fetched by this site.

Is this page affiliated with Security Headers or Scott Helme?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Scott Helme or Security Headers (securityheaders.com), named here only to describe what this checker is and is not. What Security Headers currently checks and how it grades are described on its own site -- check there for what it covers today.

Only point either tool at a system you own or are authorised to test. That rule is unchanged by which one you pick.
